title: What is the night audit in a hotel? Process, checklist and automation
summary: The night audit is the end-of-day process that closes a hotel's business date: reconciling payments and folios, posting room and tax charges, verifying res
body_text: The night audit is the end-of-day process that closes a hotel's business date: reconciling payments and folios, posting room and tax charges, verifying reservations and producing the daily reports managers rely on. Modern PMS platforms automate most of it, but understanding the steps still matters. What the night audit actually does Three jobs: financial reconciliation (every charge and payment posted to the right folio), date rollover (the PMS closes today and opens tomorrow, posting room-and-tax to in-house guests), and verification (no-shows processed, arrivals checked in or released, housekeeping statuses aligned with occupancy). A practical night-audit checklist Balance cash and card batches against the PMS. Post or verify room and tax. Process no-shows per policy (charge or release). Reconcile OTA virtual card payments. Run and file the daily reports: manager flash, occupancy and ADR, arrivals/departures, high balances. Then roll the date. How modern PMS automation changed the role Cloud PMS platforms run the audit continuously or on a schedule with no downtime, auto-posting charges and generating reports. The overnight role shifts from data entry to exception handling: chasing unbalanced folios, failed payments and mismatched OTA reservations — plus covering the desk for late arrivals. Clean audits start with clean channels Most audit exceptions trace back to distribution: manual OTA entries, unsynced cancellations, payments living outside the PMS. When your website, OTAs and payment processor feed reservations and payments into the PMS automatically, the night audit becomes a review instead of a rescue. How GuruHotel helps GuruHotel turns a hotel's official website into a direct booking channel: an AI-built site, a conversion-optimized booking engine, real-time inventory synced with your PMS (Cloudbeds direct, 280+ more via Channex) and Stripe-powered payments — commission-free on every direct reservation.

title: Operation Jailbreak and What Comes Next for Defense Integration
summary: The defense industry just received an early look at its own future, and it arrived under the banner of Operation Jailbreak, a U.S. Army hackathon that brought together hundreds of engineers across our industry to expose the gaps in sharing data across systems. What I witnessed firsthand at Fort Carson this spring was not just another interoperability demo; it was a […]
body_text: The defense industry just received an early look at its own future, and it arrived under the banner of Operation Jailbreak , a U.S. Army hackathon that brought together hundreds of engineers across our industry to expose the gaps in sharing data across systems. What I witnessed firsthand at Fort Carson this spring was not just another interoperability demo; it was a proof point that open architectures and published APIs are moving from talking points to hard requirements. For the defense technology industry, the message is clear: integration can no longer depend on heroic, one-off events. It has to be designed into systems from day one. Building the Software Bridge The most important thing about Operation Jailbreak is that it was, by design, a bridge-building exercise. The Army asked industry to do something that has traditionally been painful and slow: connect legacy command-and-control (C2) architectures, autonomous systems, and sensors through a common, well-documented interface. For this sprint, that bridge took the form of a complete, published software interface: Synchronous REST/HTTP APIs for command, configuration, and status. Asynchronous event and telemetry channels over WebSocket or publish–subscribe patterns. High-performance gRPC/Protocol Buffers for low-latency, time-sensitive data exchange. Formal specifications, including OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, and Protocol Buffer definitions, that compliant platforms could consume without a closed-door integration effort. The AV_Halo™ COMMAND submission covered node discovery, telemetry, and flight actions across these protocol layers. During the sprint, AV_Halo COMMAND was used to connect the Switchblade ® 400 from the Army’s Integrated Battle Command System – Maneuver (IBCS-M) without custom one-off integrations on either side. What It Signaled to Industry Operation Jailbreak made several points explicit. First, interoperability is now a design requirement, not a future enhancement. The Right to Integrate initiative sets the expectation that open interfaces, documented APIs, and Modular Open Systems Approach (MOSA) principles are prerequisites for participation, not optional differentiators. Second, the Army is shifting the burden of integration away from the warfighter and into the architecture. Army Chief Technology Officer Alex Miller has described the challenge bluntly: for too long, warfighters have been forced to serve as the integration point between disconnected systems. In an environment characterized by information overload, contested domains, and compressed decision timelines, that approach does not scale. Third, success will be measured less by the sophistication of any one system and more by how quickly that system can be integrated into a larger operational context. Army leadership has started to frame isolated, closed capabilities as a form of capability debt: impressive on their own but limiting when they cannot participate in a networked fight. The Army’s emerging API marketplace, and its intent to make published interfaces and MOSA compliance contractual requirements, formalize this direction. Defense software is beginning the same transition that commercial platforms made years ago: ecosystems grow around specifications, not claims of openness. A First Bridge, Not the End State It is important to recognize what Operation Jailbreak was, and what it was not. It was a focused event where government and industry deliberately built the software bridge between legacy and modern systems under a clear set of constraints and success criteria. That bridge was necessary, and it worked. But the long-term objective is not to hold recurring bridge-building events on every program. The objective was to encourage a different way of thinking: design future systems so that these bridges are inherent, not exceptional. Operation Jailbreak provided the testing ground for this new way of thinking. Using specifications and disciplined architectures with modern APIs, integration timelines can collapse from months to days compared to traditional integrations using interface control documents (ICDs). Our own experience proved that to be true. AV achieved jailbroken status in just four days by integrating AV_Halo COMMAND’s open APIs, enabling status monitoring and high-level behavioral control from IBCS-M through AV-connected systems at the tactical edge. Operation Jailbreak should be remembered as the first proof point of the operating model to come, and this level of connectivity should be the expectation, not the exception. What Built-In Interoperability Should Look Like If industry gets this right, the next generation of systems will not require ad hoc software bridges to connect into the fight. Instead, they will arrive with published, machine-readable APIs covering the full functional surface area; support for multiple interface patterns aligned with real operational use cases; and security architecture designed from the outset for shared, controlled access. They will also include requirements and test cases tied directly to interface specifications and validated continuously, not just at milestone events. Equally important, they will be built for mixed, multi-vendor environments where collaboration is normal rather than exceptional. Operation Jailbreak showed what happens when engineers from different organizations work side by side with soldiers and acquisition teams to integrate real systems while solving real mission problems such as counter-UAS and battlefield data sharing. That level of transparency and shared problem-solving needs to move from rare to routine. The Path Ahead For my team here at AV, Operation Jailbreak did not force a change in direction; it validated a strategy already centered on openness, modularity, and rapid integration. AV_Halo was built around the belief that future missions will be defined by how well systems work together, not how impressive they appear in isolation. What Operation Jailbreak added was urgency. It clarified that the organizations that can integrate quickly, share data securely, and adapt software at operational tempo will be the ones that matter most on the modern battlefield. For industry, the path forward is straightforward: design for integration as a primary requirement, publish interfaces with the same rigor applied to core mission software, and recognize that value increasingly comes from how well a system plugs into the larger architecture. For government, the task is equally clear: continue pushing openness into contracts, reward architectures that reduce operator burden and integration time, and keep creating venues where real systems can be integrated, tested, and iterated with soldiers in the loop. Operation Jailbreak showed that when the right people, architectures, and incentives come together, the integration problem looks less like a barrier and more like a solvable engineering task. The next challenge is to make that solvable task the new normal rather than a once-a-year event. ABOUT THE AUTHOR Scott Bowman is AV’s Chief Technology Officer and Senior Vice President of Global Engineering, leading the company’s technical strategy and engineering organization. With more than 18 years of experience, he specializes in robotics, autonomous systems, software, RF systems, and open architecture technologies that enable interoperable, mission-ready uncrewed systems for defense customers. JOIN THE AV MISSION AV isn’t for everyone. We hire the curious, the relentless, the mission-obsessed. The best of the best. We don’t just build defense technology—we redefine what’s possible. As the premier autonomous systems company in the U.S., AV delivers breakthrough capabilities across air, land, sea, space, and cyber. From AI-powered drones and loitering munitions to integrated autonomy and space resilience, our technologies shape the future of warfare and protect those who serve. Founded by legendary innovator Dr. Paul B. MacCready, Jr., AV has spent over 50 years pushing the boundaries of what unmanned systems can do. Our heritage includes seven platforms in the Smithsonian—but we’re not building history, we’re building what’s next. If you’re ready to build technology that matters—with speed, scale, and purpose—there’s no better place to do it than AV. title: Panorama Solara Named 2026 EdTech AI Platform of the Year by EdTech Breakthrough
summary: Panorama Education has been awarded EdTech AI Platform of the Year for 2026, highlighting its innovative AI solutions that enhance K-12 learning and support educators.
body_text: July 7, 2026 — Panorama Education, the leading platform for student support and learning in K-12 education, has been named EdTech AI Platform of the Year in the 2026 EdTech Breakthrough Awards, which recognize organizations advancing innovation across the global education technology market. This recognition follows Panorama Solara's Trendsetter Award win from EdTech Digest earlier this year, marking another milestone in the company’s continued innovation in AI-powered educator support. Now in its eighth year, the EdTech Breakthrough Awards recognize organizations driving innovation across the global education technology market. This year's program attracted more than 3,000 nominations from organizations spanning more than 20 countries, marking its largest and most competitive field to date. Panorama Solara , the solution at the heart of this recognition, is built specifically for K-12 education. Rather than a standalone AI tool, Solara securely connects AI with the systems and data districts already rely on, including student information systems, district curriculum and protocols, and the broader Panorama platform, delivering outputs that are aligned to district practices and grounded in real student context. Districts using Solara are seeing benefits that extend well beyond efficiency. Eighty-three percent of teachers report faster lesson planning, saving an average of five hours each month. More importantly, educators report reinvesting that time into supporting students. Panorama's instructional AI has also been associated with measurable academic gains, with partner districts reporting 15-17% improvements in ELA scores. Built with district governance in mind, Solara keeps district data within the Panorama ecosystem and does not use customer data to train AI models. Panorama meets FERPA, COPPA, and SOC 2 Type II standards and maintains a 1EdTech certification for data privacy, giving district leaders confidence to adopt AI responsibly while maintaining full control of their data.

title: How a 2,000-Year-Old Education Model Could Solve Today’s Learning Crisis at Scale
summary: Discover how modern microschools make elite education accessible to every learner while unlocking each student's potential and motivation.
body_text: Over two thousand years ago, a young Macedonian prince received what is arguably the best education in history. His father, King Philip II, recruited the world-famous thinker Aristotle to travel across the Mediterranean and become a personal tutor. Under the philosopher’s guidance, the boy—who would become Alexander the Great—gained deep insights into philosophy, science, and strategy, all tailored to his personal interests and strengths. This one-on-one mentorship helped shape one of the most brilliant minds of all time. Alexander’s education was personalized, rigorous, and deeply engaging —everything modern education struggles to be. But why? So many things have changed since the beginnings of our education system in the 1840’s. Today, we live in an era where information is no longer a privilege reserved for the elite. It’s abundant, free, and accessible to anyone with an internet connection. Computer systems and AI can personalize curriculum with mind-blowing efficiency, YouTube can bring the instruction to every student. But even with all this technology, kids struggle with learning more than ever. One missing puzzle piece is simple but not obvious: human motivation. As kids move through years of compulsory education, where it’s illegal to leave and you’re punished if you don’t comply, their deep-seated human impulse for autonomy starts to complain. Meanwhile, large class sizes and overstrained teachers can lead to a sense of disconnection and isolation. This leads to disengagement, which spirals as low effort leads to poor performance and a growing apathy about learning. You can see how so many high school classrooms resemble the ones Ferris Bueller might have attended. The Missing Piece: The Psychology of Learning Today, access to information isn’t the problem. The real challenge in modern education is psychological: how do we help children decide to be learners? How do we unlock the curiosity and persistence that lead to deep understanding and mastery? We believe that the psychologists studying self-determination theory have it right. Kids need autonomy, relatedness (connection), and competence in order to feel motivated to learn. Under the constraints of the traditional education system, it is very difficult and maybe impossible to provide an environment where these conditions can be met. But what if we change the constraints? This is where microschools come in. Microschools take a radically different approach to education, focusing not just on content but on the entire learning experience . They acknowledge a simple but powerful truth: humans learn best when they are engaged, supported, and empowered. What Are Microschools? Microschools are small, student-centered learning environments where kids learn in multi-age groups with a guide (not a teacher in the traditional sense). The guide acts as a mentor, coach, and cheerleader rather than a disciplinarian or lecturer. In contrast to the traditional school system, microschools allow learning environments to be nimble, adaptable, and deeply student-centered . They offer a personalized, mastery-based education that prioritizes student autonomy, curiosity, and intrinsic motivation. So why are microschools the future of education? Because they allow us to build education around the human learner. 1. Connection Over Compliance Traditional education relies on extrinsic motivators: grades, punishments, and rewards. But relationships are a prerequisite for real learning . When children feel connected to their learning environment and the people guiding them, they are far more likely to engage, persist through challenges, and develop a lifelong love of learning. Neuroscience confirms this. When kids feel disconnected, stressed, or judged, their prefrontal cortex —the part of the brain responsible for problem-solving, critical thinking, and self-regulation—goes offline . This means that traditional, pressure-based approaches to education can actually inhibit learning rather than encourage it. In microschools, students work in close-knit groups where they are known, seen, and valued . This connection fosters engagement and intrinsic motivation, leading to deeper learning and greater long-term success . 2. Personalized Learning for Mastery Imagine learning how to ride a bike with a strict time limit. You get two weeks, and at the end of that time, you either pass or fail—regardless of whether you’ve mastered the skill. Sounds ridiculous, right? Yet, that’s exactly how traditional education works. Time is held fixed and learning is the variable, when it should be the other way around. Students are expected to learn concepts on a rigid timeline, regardless of their individual needs, strengths, or challenges. Those who fall behind get labeled as "struggling" or "slow," while those who advance quickly are often held back by the pace of the class. Microschools eliminate this artificial constraint . Students don’t move on until they’ve truly mastered a concept . This mastery-based approach ensures that learning is deep and lasting rather than superficial and temporary. Each student progresses at their own pace , receiving personalized support as needed. Learning is focused on the needs and interests of the learner , making it meaningful and relevant. As a result, microschool students are able to learn more efficiently and retain information better than they would within a traditional structure. 3. Ownership of Learning In most schools, students are passive recipients of education. They sit, listen, memorize, and test. But learning isn’t something that happens to you—it’s something you do . Microschools flip this dynamic. Instead of “being schooled,” students take ownership of their learning. They make decisions about what and how they learn, guided by an adult who coaches rather than controls. Students set their own goals and track their progress. They engage in self-directed learning projects , where they explore topics that genuinely interest them. They develop a growth mindset , understanding that intelligence and ability are developed through effort and persistence. This autonomy transforms learning from something students have to do into something they want to do . 4. Putting Technology to Work As parents are increasingly frustrated with “screen-agers” consuming mindless videos in a zombie-like trance and traditional schools often struggle to integrate technology effectively, microschools leverage it in ways that truly enhance learning. The key is that technology, like all tools, has enormous potential to help humans achieve bigger goals. But it must be used properly. The small, deliberate environment can unlock this power in ways that not only keep kids safe, but equip them for a successful modern life. AI-powered tools can deliver the exact help a student needs in the way that student best receives it. Online resources give students access to the best educational content in the entire history of the world. Data-driven insights help students, guides, and parents tailor learning to each student’s needs. With deliberate use of technology, microschools can help students progress at their own pace while building genuine human connection , creating an efficient and engaging learning experience . 5. Preparing Students for the Future The one-size-fits-all model of education was designed for an industrial-era workforce, not the modern world. Today's economy values critical thinking, creativity, adaptability, and self-direction —skills that are difficult to develop in traditional schools but are common outcomes of the microschool model . Instead of simply memorizing facts and regurgitating them on multiple-choice tests, students engage in guided discussion, learning how to think, solve problems, and navigate complexity . Instead of simply following orders, they collaborate with their guide to create norms and expectations, developing self-discipline, leadership, and initiative in the process. Instead of competing for grades, students are striving for self-improvement, creating space to collaborate, innovate, and create . This kind of human-centered, future-ready education is exactly what students need to thrive in the 21st century. The Future is Small, Nimble, and Human-Centered Microschools aren’t just another educational option—they are the future of education because they address the fundamental problem that traditional schools ignore: the human psychology of learning . We know more about learning today than ever before. We understand how the brain works, what motivates students, and how to create environments that foster deep, meaningful learning. Yet, the traditional system has struggled to adopt change , clinging to outdated models that don’t serve students or society. Microschools represent a long-overdue shift —one that places students at the center of their own education, empowers them to take ownership of their learning, and prepares them for a world that values adaptability, creativity, and lifelong learning . If we want kids to thrive, we need to move beyond outdated systems and create small, connected, student-centered environments that ignite a passion for learning. Microschools do exactly that. For the first time in history, the engaging, personalized, empowering education that Aristotle provided for Alexander can become available to every child. Microschools can help make it happen. It’s time to rethink education. The future belongs to those who learn how to learn—and microschools are leading the way. 🔥 Want to learn more about microschools? Drop your email in and get access to Prenda's free overview webinar, "Microschooling 101." We'll go deeper into how microschools work, how kids learn at Prenda, and how you can start a microschool in your community. ‍

title: How to Onboard and Pay a Remote Contractor in Latin America
summary: Onboard and pay a remote contractor in Latin America the right way: classification, contracts, compliant payments, and a payout they keep.
body_text: You found the right developer in Bogota or the designer in Buenos Aires. Then comes the part that quietly breaks deals: onboarding them cleanly and paying them so the money actually arrives. In Latin America, that last step is where good hires turn into ghosted contracts. Getting it right is not complicated, it is specific. Ontop is a global payroll and payments platform that lets companies hire and pay teams in 150+ countries, so you can hire and pay contractors across Latin America without opening a local entity. Here is the full process, from the first signature to the first payout. Key takeaways US remote hiring in Latin America grew 161 percent in 2023 and kept accelerating into 2026 (Near, 2026), so onboarding fast and cleanly is a competitive edge. Misclassification is the single most expensive onboarding mistake, and in Brazil alone it can cost 3,000 to 400,000 reais per worker (Atlas HXM and Skuad, 2026). Cross-border payments moved about 179 trillion dollars in 2024 (McKinsey Global Payments Map, 2024), and still lose 3 to 7 percent to fees and FX before the worker sees the money. 62 percent of freelancers now serve international clients (Jobbers Global Freelance Payment Report, 2026), so Latin American talent expects to be paid like a global professional. Nearshore hires are filled in 7 to 28 days versus 3 to 6 months for traditional hiring (Near, 2026), so paperwork and payment setup, not talent, is the bottleneck. Ontop lets you onboard, stay compliant, and pay contractors in Latin America in a currency they control, from one platform. Why hire contractors in Latin America in 2026? Because the talent is senior, the cost is lower, and the time zones line up with the US. US remote hiring in Latin America grew 161 percent in 2023 and kept accelerating into 2026, with software engineer placements up 250 percent year over year (Near, 2026). Senior roles commonly cost 50 to 70 percent less than in the US, and nearshore hires are filled in 7 to 28 days instead of 3 to 6 months. Ontop's own platform data in 2026 shows Colombia and Argentina as its two largest markets for Latin American talent, which is exactly where getting the payout right matters most. The region is easy to hire in; the discipline is in paying cleanly. How do you classify a contractor in Latin America? Classify by how the person actually works, not by the label on the contract. A genuine contractor sets their own hours, uses their own tools, and can work for other clients. If you control their schedule and methods like an employee, most Latin American labor authorities will treat them as one, with back taxes attached. What happens if you get it wrong? Misclassification can trigger retroactive social contributions, fines, and severance claims in the worker's country. It is the risk that turns a cheap hire into an expensive lesson. What are the penalties for getting classification wrong in Latin America? Steep, and rising. In Brazil, treating an employee as a contractor can cost 3,000 to 400,000 reais per worker (Atlas HXM and Skuad, 2026), and across the region a reclassification brings retroactive social contributions, severance, and fines. The savings from calling someone a contractor disappear the moment a labor authority disagrees, so classify honestly and keep the relationship genuinely independent. What should a contractor agreement include? A strong agreement names the scope, deliverables, payment terms, currency, and confidentiality in writing. State the amount, the currency, and the payment date explicitly, because ambiguity on payday is the fastest way to lose trust with a new contractor. Keep it simple and specific. A one-page agreement everyone understands beats a ten-page template nobody reads. What documents do you need to onboard a contractor? Three things, on file from day one: a signed contractor agreement, the tax or identification documentation the contractor's country requires, and a clean invoicing process so every payment has a paper trail. Assembling these after an audit begins is far harder than collecting them up front, and a missing document is what turns a routine review into a problem. How do you stay compliant when paying contractors abroad? Collect the right tax documentation for cross-border work, keep clean records of every payment, and adapt to each country's rules. Requirements differ across Mexico, Colombia, Argentina, and Brazil, so a process that flexes per jurisdiction keeps you audit-ready without a finance team in every market. You can compare what compliant hiring actually costs on the pricing page before committing to a method. How long does it take to onboard a contractor in Latin America? Days, not months, when the process is ready. Nearshore hires in Latin America are filled in 7 to 28 days versus the 3 to 6 months of traditional hiring (Near, 2026), and onboarding a contractor is faster than an employee because there is no entity or benefits setup. The delay, when there is one, comes from payment setup, not from the talent. What is the best way to pay a contractor in Latin America? The best method pays in full, on time, in a currency the contractor controls. International wires are familiar but slow and heavy on fees. Payout platforms are faster but often convert against the worker. A workforce platform pays into an account the contractor holds, so they decide when to convert. Method Speed Watch for International wire Slow Flat fees plus FX markup Payout platform Faster Forced currency conversion Workforce platform Fast Confirm worker currency control How do you keep your best contractors from leaving? Pay them like the money matters, because to them it does. A designer in Buenos Aires cannot plan rent around a payment that might clear next Thursday. When a payout is late or shaved by conversion, they feel it immediately, and they start answering other recruiters. If cash flow gaps are the problem, Paycheck Advance gives workers early access to earnings, and an Ontop Global Account lets them hold and move dollars on their terms. Frequently asked questions Why hire contractors in Latin America? Senior talent at 50 to 70 percent lower cost than the US, overlapping time zones, and roles filled in 7 to 28 days rather than months (Near, 2026). How long does onboarding take? Days when the process is ready. The slow part is payment setup, not the hire itself. Can I pay a Latin American contractor in US dollars? Yes, and many prefer it, as long as they can hold those dollars and convert on their own terms. Do I need a legal entity to hire a contractor in Latin America? No. You can engage an independent contractor directly with a proper agreement, or use a workforce platform to handle payments and documentation without a local entity. What is the biggest hidden cost? The FX spread and fees on each cross-border payout, which can quietly take 3 to 7 percent before the contractor sees the money (McKinsey Global Payments Report, 2026). Closing thoughts Onboarding is a form. Retention is a payment. Get the classification right, put the terms in writing, and pay in a currency the contractor controls, and Latin America becomes one of the easiest places in the world to build a team. Miss the payout, and the best people quietly leave. Book a demo to see how Ontop onboards and pays contractors across Latin America.

title: Glide Pricing: Current Plans, Real Costs, and Jet Admin Alternatives (July 2026)
summary: Trying to pin down what you will actually pay for a Glide app? You are not alone. Glide pricing has changed multiple times, and the numbers you find across the web often contradict each other. This guide cuts through the noise with verified plan details, real cost drivers, and a
body_text: Trying to pin down what you will actually pay for a Glide app? You are not alone. Glide pricing has changed multiple times, and the numbers you find across the web often contradict each other. This guide cuts through the noise with verified plan details, real cost drivers, and a practical comparison with alternatives-including Jet Admin-so you can make a confident decision for your next internal tool or customer portal. Key Takeaways This guide is based on Glide's public pricing page, checked in July 2026. Glide's published pricing currently ranges from a free plan through several paid plans up to a custom-priced enterprise tier. Here is what matters most before you commit: The main cost drivers are not just the list price. How many signed-in users you have, which data sources you connect (especially external data sources like Google Sheets or SQL), and how many monthly updates your apps generate will determine your real bill. Glide's free plan is best treated as a sandbox for personal use and learning. The Explorer, Maker, Business, and Enterprise plans are designed for production business apps, each with different plan limits on users, updates, and data rows. Usage-based pricing-updates, additional user seats, and governance add-ons-can materially increase total cost beyond the headline subscription. Teams building secure customer or partner portals should compare Glide with alternatives like Jet Admin before committing. This article closes with a practical decision guide and a comparison of when Glide vs Jet Admin makes more sense for internal tools and external-facing portals. Quick Answer: How Much Does Glide Cost in 2026? Pricing checked on Glide's official site on July 16, 2026. Glide's current pricing plan lineup includes five tiers: Free, Explorer, Maker, Business, and Enterprise. Glide's setup encourages scalability from personal to enterprise applications, but the sticker price is only the starting point. Free plan: $0/month. Best for learning, prototyping, and personal projects-limited to one app with restricted updates and features. Explorer plan: Starts around $19/month with annual billing ($25/month if billed monthly). Aimed at individuals testing a published app with a small audience. Maker plan: Around $49/month billed annually. Glide's Maker Plan costs $60/month for individuals paying month-to-month, with limited app updates. Suits solo builders creating multiple published apps. Business plan: Approximately $199/month billed annually ($249/month on monthly billing). Built for teams needing unlimited apps, more users, and deeper integrations. Some sources reference a legacy pricing of $310/month for larger organizations; always verify against the current plan. Enterprise plan: Custom pricing (sales-quoted). The Enterprise Plan pricing is customized based on usage needs, with some historical references suggesting it starts at $750/month. The base price on every paid tier covers a defined number of signed-in users and a monthly pool of updates. Going beyond these is where many teams see higher-than-expected bills. Monthly costs in Glide are influenced by the type of plan and user requirements, so a simple headline number rarely tells the full story. Why Different Sites Show Different Glide Prices If you have searched "glide pricing" recently, you have probably noticed wildly inconsistent numbers. That is because many blog posts still reference legacy Glide pricing plans-tiers like the starter plan ($25/month), a Pro plan ($45/month), or an older business plan at $310/month-that no longer exist under those names as of 2026. Glide has restructured its plans multiple times. The current catalog (Free, Explorer, Maker, Business, Enterprise) was introduced around November 2025 , replacing earlier naming conventions and shifting usage limits, update quotas, and seat definitions. Always confirm details on Glide's live pricing page before finalizing your business plan or budget. Seat definitions, update limits, and data-source rules can change without much notice. Throughout this article, we clearly separate facts verified from Glide's page as of July 2026 from historical or third-party references to avoid confusion. Glide Pricing Plans at a Glance Below is a quick orientation across all of Glide's pricing plans, from free to enterprise. The Glide pricing tier includes Free, Explorer, Maker, Business, and Enterprise. Higher-tier plans unlock additional features and integrations at each step. Plan Price (Annual Billing) Included Users Monthly Updates Apps Best For Free $0 1 editor Minimal (drafts only) 1 app Learning, prototyping Explorer ~$19/mo 2 editors, up to 100 personal users 250 1 published app Solo builders testing ideas Maker ~$49/mo 2 editors, unlimited personal users 500 3 published apps Individuals shipping real apps Business ~$199/mo 10 editors, 30 business users 5,000 Unlimited apps Teams, production deployments Enterprise Custom Custom Custom Unlimited Large orgs, compliance-heavy Some sources also reference a team plan priced at $125/month for companies with collaborative needs (up to 5 editors); this may reflect a legacy or transitional tier. Verify the latest naming directly with Glide. Key distinctions across tiers: API access (via the Glide API), custom domains, SSO, and advanced security features are generally limited to Business and enterprise plans. Custom branding and the ability to remove Glide's logo require at least the Maker tier. Inside Each Glide Plan: Limits, Pros, and Tradeoffs This section breaks down each plan beyond the marketing bullets, focusing on practical limits that affect real deployments. Free Plan Glide's free plan allows users to create one app with limited features. It is suitable for personal projects and learning purposes-think sandbox, not production. Limits include: One published app with Glide branding Up to 25,000 data rows via Glide Tables Community support only; no custom domain No workflow automations or external integrations Glide requires a database before building apps, and on the free plan that database is limited to Glide Tables. This is rarely enough for customer-facing or internal production tools. Explorer Plan At ~$19/month (annual billing), Explorer gives you one published app, 250 monthly updates, and support for Glide AI. You get two editors and up to 100 personal users. It is a step up for solo builders who want to ship a web app to a small audience but do not need advanced features. Maker Plan The Maker Plan costs $60/month for individuals on monthly billing (~$49 with annual billing) and offers 5 GB of storage. You get three published apps, unlimited personal users, and 500 monthly updates. Custom domains and custom branding become available here, making it the entry point for polished apps. Tradeoff: 500 updates can be consumed quickly if your app relies on external data sources or frequent automations. Team Plan Some references cite a team plan at $125/month for companies, allowing real-time collaboration with up to 5 editors. This tier supports more powerful data sources (Google Sheets, Airtable, Excel) and makes sense for small teams building internal tools or lightweight customer portals. Availability of this tier should be confirmed on Glide's current pricing page. Business and Enterprise Plans The Business Plan includes 500 GB of data and priority support. It ships with 30 included business email users; each additional user beyond that costs roughly $5/month with annual billing ($6/month on monthly billing). Update limits jump to 5,000/month, and you get unlimited apps plus support for advanced features like express support and more data source types. Business plans include a specific number of users with options for additional users, making them suitable for a 40-seat internal field operations app or a growing customer portal. The Enterprise Plan pricing is customized based on usage needs and unlocks SSO, dedicated account management, SQL and BigQuery data sources, and higher row limits. Enterprise plans are the only tier with custom terms for governance-heavy deployments. How Glide Measures Usage: Updates, Users, and Data Sources Glide's pricing is not just about seats. Updates and how you use data sources can be just as important in your total cost. An "update" is consumed when a workflow runs, when external data sources (like Google Sheets or Airtable) sync, when the Glide AI processes a request, or when any third-party API call fires. Updates are not the same as page views, sessions, or app opens. Glide supports multiple data sources including Google Sheets and Airtable, and every write or sync to those sources can consume updates. User types and how they count: Internal users: employees with logins, counted as editors or team members External users: customers or partners signing in, typically counted as business email users on the Business plan Public users or anonymous visitors browsing a public app may not count against seat limits, but they also cannot trigger authenticated actions Data source impact: Glide Tables and big tables (Glide's internal storage) tend to be more generous with update consumption than external data sources. If your app relies heavily on Google Sheets or Airtable syncing, expect higher update usage. Data updates in Glide are charged if they exceed monthly limits at a rate of $0.02 per extra update. Numeric example: If you run an inventory app with 5,000 product changes per day, that is roughly 110,000 updates per month. Even on the Business plan (5,000 included), you would face around 105,000 overage updates-costing approximately $2,100 in overage alone. Factor in user growth and integration complexity when evaluating whether Glide is worth it for long-term use. Total Cost of Ownership: What Really Makes Glide Expensive (or Cheap) The list price on Glide's pricing page is only one part of the total cost. Actual spend depends on usage, governance needs, and how your teams work. Glide's pricing tiers can lead to unexpected additional charges if you are not careful. Core cost drivers beyond the subscription: Number of signed-in users, especially external customers. Growing from 30 to 300 business email users on the Business plan adds roughly $1,350/month in seat costs alone. Monthly updates beyond the included quota. Apps that consume updates through heavy automations, external syncs, or Glide AI requests can push overage charges well past the base fee. Number of apps and environments. Needing separate dev, staging, and production setups may require higher tiers or multiple workspaces. Native mobile distribution. Glide apps cannot be published directly to app stores, so teams needing native iOS or Android apps must layer on third-party services-an added cost and complexity. Support and governance. Priority support, SSO, and audit capabilities are gated to Business or Enterprise, pushing you into higher tiers even with modest usage. Scaling example: A simple internal dashboard for 10 users on the Maker plan may cost ~$49/month. Scale that same concept to a customer-facing portal with 500 sign-ins and frequent data writes, and you could easily land at $2,000+/month on the Business plan once you factor in extra users and update overages. Back-of-the-envelope checklist before committing: How many users will sign in monthly (internal vs external)? How many data writes/syncs will your app trigger per day? Which data sources are required (Glide Tables, spreadsheets, SQL)? Do you need SSO, audit logs, or compliance controls? Will you need more than one environment or staging setup? Is Glide Worth It for Your Use Case? The real question is: is Glide worth it for your specific workflow and risk tolerance? There is no universal answer. Where Glide tends to be a strong fit: Small to mid-sized internal tools and data-driven dashboards CRUD apps where you control the user base and data sources are fairly simple Rapid prototyping when you need to build apps quickly with no coding required Structured data management for small teams using spreadsheets as a backend Where Glide is less compelling: Public consumer mobile apps that need Apple App Store or Google Play distribution (Glide outputs a web app, not native apps) Apps needing native device capabilities or native code execution Highly customized UI layouts-Glide's customization options are limited to set templates, and teams wanting more customization may hit walls quickly Scenarios requiring an unlimited number of external users without per-seat costs Glide can be cost-effective early on (free or Maker plan) but may become less attractive as the number of external users, integrations, and required update limits grows. Use this quick self-assessment: count your expected users, list your critical data sources, document compliance needs, and estimate your iteration speed. If the numbers stay modest, Glide makes sense. If they do not, keep reading. Glide vs Native and Low-Code App Builders (Pricing Perspective) Glide sits firmly in the web app and internal tool camp. Some alternatives focus on native mobile apps or more traditional low-code approaches, and the pricing models differ significantly. No-code native app builders (e.g., Adalo): Adalo starts at $36/month, cheaper than Glide's $60/month Maker plan. Adalo creates true native apps for iOS and Android that can be published directly to app stores and Google Play-something Glide requires third-party services for. Adalo allows unlimited database records on paid plans and offers extensive design customization compared to Glide. However, Adalo may be less suited for data-heavy internal dashboards or apps backed by existing databases. Low-code business app platforms: Tools like Retool or other no code tools in this category typically charge per end-user or per environment, not per update. This can make costs more predictable for teams with high-volume data operations but modest user counts. Some platforms also offer self-hosted deployment, which Glide does not. Key cost differences to evaluate: Does the platform output native apps or android apps, or only web apps? Is pricing per app, per seat, or per environment? How does it handle usage-API calls, workflow runs, or storage limits? Teams needing direct app-store distribution should evaluate whether paying for Glide plus a third-party wrapper is cheaper or more complex than using a native-first platform. For internal tools, the calculus is different: Glide's speed of deployment often offsets its usage-based billing, at least at smaller scale. When Glide's Pricing and Limits Stop Making Sense Some teams start happily on Glide but later run into scaling, governance, or pricing pain points. Here are common breaking points: Rapid growth in external users. Every customer or partner who signs in becomes a paid seat on the Business plan. A customer-support portal that grows from 100 to 5,000 users turns a $199/month subscription into a multi-thousand-dollar monthly expense in seat costs alone. Heavy reliance on external data sources. Apps syncing frequently with Google Sheets, Airtable, or SQL databases can spike update costs far beyond the included quota. A logistics app that writes thousands of app updates per hour could burn through the entire monthly allocation in days. Complex permission models. If your new app requires enterprise-grade governance-row-level access control, SSO, audit logs-you may be forced into Enterprise even though your usage is otherwise modest. Operational risks to consider: Migration cost if you later outgrow Glide. Data locked in Glide Tables is less portable than data sitting in a standard PostgreSQL or MySQL database. Lock-in around proprietary tables versus portable databases should factor into early plan selection. Revisit your assumptions about more users, data sources, and compliance requirements annually-not just at initial launch. What looks affordable today may not hold up under growth. Glide Alternatives for Internal Tools and Portals Glide is only one of several options for building internal tools, admin panels, and customer portals without heavy custom development. Alternatives generally fall into a few buckets: Spreadsheet-driven no-code tools: Platforms like Softr or AppSheet let you build apps on top of existing data in Google Sheets or Airtable. Pricing tends to be seat-based with fewer usage-based variables, which can make budgeting simpler for small teams. Visual app builders focused on native mobile: Tools like Adalo or FlutterFlow output native iOS and Android apps. They charge per app or per user rather than per update, and they handle app building for app stores directly. Trade-off: they may offer less support for complex backend logic or multi-source data models. Internal-tool platforms (e.g., Jet Admin): Platforms in this category connect directly to existing databases, SaaS APIs, and warehouses to build secure, branded portals and dashboards. Pricing models in this bucket tend to be more seat-based or workspace-based, avoiding the update-quota friction that defines Glide's approach. When evaluating other no code tools, look for: support for your existing data (databases, SaaS APIs), pricing predictability, governance features (RBAC, SSO), and deployment options (cloud vs self-hosted). Each factor can tilt the decision. Where Jet Admin Fits vs Glide (and When to Consider Switching) Jet Admin is a no-code/low-code platform for building secure business apps on top of existing databases, APIs, spreadsheets, and SaaS tools. It is oriented toward secure internal tools and external customer/partner portals built directly on your existing data, rather than a spreadsheet-first app building approach. Data source flexibility: Jet Admin connects to a wide range of data sources-PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, BigQuery, Snowflake, Firebase, REST/GraphQL APIs, plus SaaS tools like Stripe, Salesforce, HubSpot, and Zendesk-as documented on its integrations page . This can reduce the need to replicate data into proprietary tables, avoiding the "update tax" that comes with syncing external sources in Glide. Governance and portal capabilities: Jet Admin's customer-portal documentation describes building branded portals with controlled user access, orchestrating workflows and automations across tools, and using 100+ drag-and-drop UI components. Role-based access and data separation for multi-tenant setups are part of the platform's documented capabilities. When to evaluate Jet Admin alongside Glide: You need secure self-service portals on top of production databases, not spreadsheet replicas Multi-source data models are central to your business needs You want to avoid being billed by per-update quotas that vary based on sync frequency You need to support a large number of external users without per-seat escalation Visit Jet Admin's customer-portal overview and integrations catalog for up-to-date capabilities and pricing details. Decision Guide: Choosing the Right Glide Plan (or an Alternative) Here is a practical decision flow based on common personas: Solo maker validating an idea: Start with Glide's free plan or Explorer plan. You get one app, minimal cost, and enough room to test a concept. The pricing plan risk is low. If the idea gains traction, upgrade to the Maker plan for custom apps with branding and a custom domain. Operations team building internal dashboards: The Maker plan or a team plan (if available) covers three published apps and enough updates for light-to-moderate usage. Watch your update consumption closely if you connect external spreadsheets. If your team needs more editors or broader data source support, the Business plan is the natural next step. Customer success team launching a customer portal: This is where Glide's pricing can get tricky. External users on the Business plan cost ~$5/month each. If you expect hundreds of users, model that cost carefully-and evaluate Jet Admin as an alternative that is purpose-built for branded portals on existing data. IT/product team standardizing custom apps across the organization: Enterprise plans with custom terms, SSO, and unlimited usage are likely necessary. Get a sales quote and compare it with platforms like Jet Admin that may offer more predictable pricing at scale, especially if your data already lives in SQL databases. Pre-commitment checklist: What data sources will you connect (Glide Tables, Google Sheets, SQL, APIs)? How many users will you have by end of year one, year three? Do you have governance or compliance requirements (SSO, audit logs, education email domain restrictions)? Do you need a mobile app for app stores, or is a web app sufficient? Are you comfortable with update-based billing, or do you prefer flat-rate models? Conclusion: How to Move Forward with Glide Pricing Glide can be a solid fit for certain app types and team sizes, but its update- and seat-based pricing requires careful planning. The platform excels at helping small teams build apps fast with no coding required-but the cost of scaling, especially for external-facing portals, can surprise you. Always verify current Glide pricing and limits before finalizing your budget. Names, user caps, and usage rules have changed multiple times historically, and they will likely change again. Model at least two or three realistic growth scenarios-current year, +1 year, +3 years-to understand how total cost evolves. If you are building secure internal tools or external customer portals, also explore Jet Admin's customer-portal overview and integrations catalog to see whether its data-first approach and governance capabilities better fit your roadmap. Treat this analysis as a living part of your tooling strategy. Revisit your pricing plan whenever product or compliance requirements shift, and do not let a single line item in a pricing table drive a decision that affects your entire stack. FAQ: Common Questions About Glide Pricing and Plans This FAQ covers edge cases and clarifications not fully addressed in the main sections. All answers are consistent with Glide's official pricing and documentation as of July 2026; details may change over time. Does Glide charge per user, per app, or per workspace? Glide's pricing blends several dimensions. Each pricing plan includes a base fee covering a set number of signed-in users, limits on the number of apps or pages per workspace, and usage limits like updates. On the Business plan, for example, you get 30 included business email users and unlimited apps, but each additional user beyond 30 costs extra. Internal users (editors, team members) and external users (customers, partners) may be counted differently depending on the tier. A public user browsing without signing in typically does not count against seat limits. Teams with many external customers should pay close attention to user definitions and confirm with Glide's current plan documentation before launching large-scale portals. Can I Stay on an Older Glide Plan if My Pricing Changed? Some long-time customers may still be on legacy pricing plans (like earlier Starter or Pro tiers). Availability of these grandfathered plans depends entirely on Glide's current policies. Do not assume you can sign up for historical plans mentioned in older blog posts-new workspaces are constrained to the current catalog. If you are an existing customer seeking clarification about legacy vs new plan migration, reach out directly to Glide support. Yes free trial periods or promotional pricing from past campaigns may no longer apply to new accounts. What Happens if I Exceed Glide's Monthly Updates? Most paid plans include a fixed pool of monthly updates. When that quota is exhausted, Glide temporarily stops executing workflows , external data sources stop syncing, and Glide AI returns no response. Extra updates are billed at approximately $0.02 per update if you enable unlimited updates on your plan. Teams with volatile or high-volume workloads-real-time IoT feeds, high-traffic CRMs, apps that consume updates heavily through automations-should monitor update consumption closely. Consider architectures that reduce write frequency or batch operations to stay within your current plan's quota. Is There a Truly Free Way to Run Production Apps on Glide? While Glide offers a free plan, it is best for learning, prototyping, and small internal tools for personal use. Glide's free plan allows one app with limited updates, Glide branding, and restricted customization. Running a production-grade external app on the free plan usually runs into issues like inability to scale user counts, limited data rows, and no custom domain. Teams needing a no-cost option for real production traffic should reevaluate their requirements or compare with other platforms' free tiers. Plan for a paid plan as soon as the app gains traction. App building for non profit or education use cases may also benefit from exploring whether Glide offers any special programs tied to an education email domain. How Should Glide Pricing Factor into My Business Plan? Incorporate Glide subscription and expected overage costs directly into your business plan, alongside hosting, support, and maintenance budgets. Model at least three scenarios: conservative (few users, low updates), expected (moderate growth, regular integrations), and aggressive (rapid user acquisition, heavy automations). This reveals how Glide's pricing plans scale over time and where breakpoints occur. Document a potential migration path-including options like Jet Admin for internal tools and portals-so that future plan changes or enterprise pricing shifts do not derail your long-term product and financial planning. Revisit this model quarterly, not just at launch.

title: TCFD guidance not "necessarily clear" as mandatory disclosures loom
summary: Sam Alberti of Accountancy Age reports: Businesses are at risk of being too cautious with disclosures due to the lack of clarity. First reported in Accountancy Age. The UK’s introduction of a mandate on climate-related financial disclosures could pose an initial challenge to organisations due to unclear guidance, according to Justin Elks, risk consulting partner at Crowe.
body_text: Sam Alberti of Accountancy Age reports: Businesses are at risk of being too cautious with disclosures due to the lack of clarity. First reported in Accountancy Age . The UK’s introduction of a mandate on climate-related financial disclosures could pose an initial challenge to organisations due to unclear guidance, according to Justin Elks, risk consulting partner at Crowe. “What it means to comply isn’t necessarily clear. There’s a lot of recommendations, a lot of choices of metrics. “Within the guidance, there is a lot of development that’s needed.” As of April 6, 2022, more than 1,300 of the UK’s largest businesses will be legally required to disclose climate-related financial information in line with the Taskforce on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) recommendations . This will make the UK the first G20 nation to enshrine mandatory TCFD-aligned requirements into law. But despite the recommendations’ overarching purpose to standardise and simplify the disclosure of climate-related information , an inevitable period of uncertainty will follow the initial rollout, Elks says “Everybody’s learning. The methodology is evolving. It’s an evolving picture and people are still getting to grips with it and moving it forward. So that creates some difficulty in terms of pitching what you put out there.” Elks also expresses concern that, because TCFD-aligned disclosures have never been legally mandated before and, therefore, looking to peers may not be a viable strategy in the early stages. “While there is TCFD disclosure out there, it’s typically updated on an annual basis, so that can be a bit of a challenge.” He goes on to argue that this lack of precedent could create a tendency for caution among businesses, which may prove counterproductive. “I think there’s a danger that companies can be too ambitious and therefore they’re criticised later if they don’t achieve their ambitions. But equally, there are dangers of being unambitious and being seen to be out of line with your peer group. “The answer to this isn’t just to be really cautious and disclose nothing, because you could find yourself at a competitive disadvantage.” The TCFD was created in 2015 by the Financial Stability Board with a view to standardising the disclosure of climate-related financial risk. In June 2017, it went on to publish its final recommendations. At the heart of the guidance is four “core elements” of climate-related financial disclosures: governance, strategy, risk management and metrics and targets. But according to Andromeda Wood, VP regulatory strategy at Workiva, businesses who struggle to meet the expectations of these pillars will find compliance challenging. “If businesses are unable to work towards these pillars, then even producing compliant disclosures could be a challenge,” she says. “They will need to disclose the metrics and targets used for measuring performance and declare how they expect those risks will impact the resiliency of their corporate strategies as well as their organisations’ financial performance.” A learning curve for businesses Wood argues that organisations must respond to these challenges by proactively adjusting processes and workstreams. “Businesses should be assessing their processes to identify the gaps and implement technology where possible so that they can streamline workstreams,” she says. “This will enable them to disclose their industry-specific metrics, individual targets and KPIs for measuring progress against targets.” Simon Weaver, partner and co-head of climate risk and strategy at KPMG, thinks the first port of call for businesses ahead of the April deadline is to establish clarity on what needs to be reported this year. For accounting periods starting in 2021, UK premium-listed companies need to report on the TCFD recommendations and guidance published up until 2020. Accounting periods starting in 2022 will see new rules included in the TCFD guidelines to obtain information on climate transition plans and how companies will reach their net-zero targets. “The key recommendation would be for companies to get a cross-functional working group together, agree on the impacts, and agree who will lead on bringing this cross-functional thinking together.” Weaver also argues that the CEO and CFO need to be intimately involved with these processes to “set the tone right from the top”. This is echoed by Elks, who argues that technology is far less significant than “the organisation itself” when it comes to TCFD-compliance. “The fundamentals for me of what a company should be doing are around understanding its risks, developing clear strategy, developing an effective transition plan, and moving forward on that basis,” he says. “Then disclosure comes from the quality of what you’re actually doing, rather than becoming a piece of greenwashing.” Elks also argues that advisers can be a critical enabler of these developments for organisations. “Helping companies to work out what their transition plan is, what their targets should be, and what they should do to address climate change is key. “There’s a lot more to it beneath the surface than just adding another bit of disclosure to the finance team’s workload. For the latest news and information, visit The Workiva Newsroom . title: Security without the Spectacle
summary: Scale detection, response, and threat hunting beyond headcount. Build AI agents across your entire security stack. Improve coverage, cut MTTR, and eliminate manual & repetitive security work.
body_text: Why would anyone want to start an AI security company? It’s a fair question, and one we asked ourselves many times. Security is a notoriously hard market: crowded, cynical, and full of products that overpromise and underdeliver. But we also knew, from our years embedded in the trenches with the world’s best security teams, that the real work of security was still painfully manual, fragmented, and exhausting. We believed there had to be a better way, and we wanted to build it. The cybersecurity industry has no shortage of bold claims. Every year, the RSA Conference floor fills with vendors promising “next-generation solutions” and “AI-powered detection.” But most of these products are little more than last decade’s SIEM tools dressed up with superficial LLM features. The truth is: security teams don’t need more dashboards or "insights." They need time. The State of Security Today Security organizations remain bogged down by: Alert fatigue: Hours lost investigating false positives while genuine threats risk slipping through. Context switching: Investigations that require jumping between 5 to 10 disconnected tools just to gather the basics. Documentation overhead: Endless manual reporting that turns skilled threat hunters into technical scribes. AI gives us a chance to reimagine the solutions to these challenges. Not by replacing humans, but by building tools that work with them, seamlessly integrated into their workflows. Why Cotool Cotool is built for practitioners: we're not just another dashboard. We’ve been inspired by the success of AI coding tools like Cursor and Windsurf, which don’t aim to replace engineers but instead help them become 10x more productive. Cotool applies the same product philosophy to security teams: augmenting practitioners with powerful tools that eliminate repetitive work and free them to focus on what truly matters. Who We Are We started Cotool in 2025 after years of building security tools for some of the world’s most demanding organizations. Max Pollard, CEO: Formerly led the forward deployed engineering team at Material Security, scaling it from 1 to 8 engineers. Previously Solutions Engineering at Okta. Eddie Conk, CPO & Head of AI: Led ML engineering at Material Security, training large-scale phishing detection models. Previously ML Engineering at Apple. Logan Carmody, CTO: Technical lead for phishing protection at Material Security, architecting much of the core Phishing Detection infrastructure of the product. Previously Staff SWE at LinkedIn focused on infrastructure. We believe security should be empowering, not exhausting. Our mission is simple: help security teams reclaim their time and focus on what truly matters. Best job in the world. Back to work.
